planting.note: Plant offsets or rooted leaf cuttings in spring in lean, gravelly soil in full sun; this desert native tolerates more cold and drought than most Echeveria once established.

directions: Native to the Chihuahuan Desert of West Texas and northern Mexico, this low rosette produces narrow, pointed, grey-green leaves that often take on a reddish-bronze cast under intense sun and dry conditions. Thin, wiry flower stalks rise above the foliage in summer, carrying small, slender red-and-yellow blooms favored by hummingbirds. Grow in gritty, mineral soil with excellent drainage, watering only occasionally, and keep the crown dry over winter. It tolerates brief dips below freezing better than most echeverias, provided the soil is kept dry.

common_name: Toliman Echeveria (Frosted White Clustering Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Separate offsets in spring and plant in sharply drained, mineral soil in full sun; this clustering species needs excellent drainage and resents winter wet.

directions: Collected from limestone hills near Toliman in Queretaro, Mexico, this compact species forms tight clusters of small rosettes coated in a dense white, powdery farina that rubs off easily with handling. The chalky-white leaves are broad and pointed, often blushing pink at the tips under strong sun and cool nights. Coral-pink, bell-shaped flowers appear on short stalks above the foliage in late winter. Keep off overhead watering to preserve the delicate farina coating and let the soil dry fully between waterings.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in well-drained soil and give a hanging basket or elevated bed so the trailing stems can cascade; protect from direct hot afternoon sun.

directions: Native to cloud forest margins in Chiapas, Mexico and Guatemala, this unusual species develops long, branching stems that sprawl or trail rather than forming a tight solitary rosette, carrying small clusters of thick, glossy green leaves along their length. Tubular orange-red flowers are produced in loose clusters in summer. Because it comes from shadier, more humid habitat than most echeverias, it prefers filtered light and slightly more frequent watering, though the soil should still dry between waterings. Stems root readily where they touch soil, making it easy to propagate by cuttings or layering.

common_name: Moran's Echeveria (Compact Grey-Green Oaxacan Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; named for botanist Reid Moran, this species is best suited to bright, dry conditions typical of its Oaxacan habitat.

directions: Found on rocky slopes in Oaxaca, Mexico, this species forms a solitary to loosely clustering rosette of thick, spoon-shaped, grey-green leaves with a faint pink blush along the margins. Coral-orange flowers rise on slender stalks in spring, held well above the foliage. Water deeply and then allow the soil to dry out completely, since the species is prone to rot in consistently damp conditions. It offsets slowly compared to many echeverias, so established clumps take a few seasons to fill in.

common_name: Split-Petaled Echeveria (Silvery Rosette with Orange-Red Flowers)

planting.note: Plant offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in mineral, fast-draining soil in full sun; this high-elevation Hidalgo native appreciates cooler summer nights and a brief dry winter rest.

directions: Native to rocky outcrops in Hidalgo, Mexico, this species forms a short-stemmed rosette of silvery grey-green leaves, their edges often tinged pink in strong light. Its common name refers to the notched, two-lobed tips of the tubular orange-red flowers that appear on branched stalks in late spring and summer. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil and water only when the mix is fully dry, since it comes from a seasonally dry montane habitat. It tolerates light frost better than lowland Mexican species provided the soil stays dry.

common_name: Dwarf Hidalgo Echeveria (Tiny Blue-Green Clustering Succulent)

planting.note: Separate the small offsets in spring and plant in shallow trays or rock garden pockets of gritty, mineral soil; this miniature species suits troughs and dish gardens as readily as open ground.

directions: One of the smallest echeverias in cultivation, this Hidalgo native forms dense mats of tiny, tightly packed rosettes only an inch or two across, the thick blue-green leaves often flushed pink at the tips. Small coral-pink, bell-shaped flowers appear on short stalks just above the foliage in spring. Because of its diminutive size it is especially prone to rot if overwatered, so let the soil dry completely between waterings and keep it in full sun with excellent air movement. It spreads slowly into a low, carpeting clump as offsets accumulate around the parent rosettes.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; as the stem lengthens over time it benefits from staking or a low, wide container to stay upright.

directions: Named for American botanist Cyrus Pringle, this Oaxacan species develops an upright stem over time, topped by an open rosette of elongated, pointed, grey-green leaves with a soft waxy bloom. Orange-red flowers appear on branched stalks held above the foliage in the warmer months. Older plants naturally lose their lower leaves as the stem lengthens, giving the plant a small shrub-like profile distinct from the stemless echeverias already common in cultivation. Grow in full sun with sharply drained soil and let it dry fully between waterings.

common_name: Parras Echeveria (Small Blue-Grey Coahuila Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Separate offsets in spring and plant in very gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; collected from higher, cooler desert elevations, it tolerates more cold and dryness than many of its lowland relatives.

directions: Native to limestone slopes near Parras in Coahuila, Mexico, this small species forms compact, solitary to sparingly clustering rosettes of thick, blue-grey leaves with fine reddish tips. Pink-and-yellow bicolor flowers are carried on short, arching stalks in late spring. Its high-desert origin makes it more tolerant of brief cold snaps and prolonged drought than tropical lowland echeverias, though it still needs sharp drainage to avoid winter rot. Keep it on the dry side year-round and reserve the richest sun for the best leaf color.

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; cool nights and bright light bring out the strongest pink blush on the frosted foliage.

directions: This Oaxacan species forms a solitary rosette of broad, powder-coated leaves in a soft dusty blue-green that flushes rosy pink across the upper surface and margins in cool, bright conditions. Orange flowers tinged yellow at the mouth rise on slender stalks above the foliage in spring. Like other heavily farina-coated echeverias, it is best watered from below or around the base of the rosette to keep the powdery bloom intact. Allow the soil to dry completely between waterings and protect from hard frost and winter rain.

planting.note: Plant offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in lean, gritty soil in full sun to light shade; the long leaves are brittle and detach easily, so handle new plantings with care.

directions: True to its name, this species forms a low, wide rosette of unusually long, narrow, blue-green leaves that can stretch well beyond the leaf length typical of most echeverias in cultivation. Leaf tips and margins often take on a reddish tinge under bright light, and the rosette offsets to form small, open clusters over time. Orange-red flowers appear on tall, arching stalks in summer, rising well above the foliage. Grow in sharply drained soil and water only once the mix has dried out fully, since the elongated leaves are more prone to splitting if kept too wet.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant offsets in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this large hybrid benefits from a sturdy container or bed to support its substantial rosette.

directions: A robust Echeveria gibbiflora-type hybrid, Pollux grows on a stout stem into a broad rosette of thick, wavy-edged leaves finished in a soft silvery-pink powder coat that deepens toward rose and lavender in cool weather and bright sun. Tall, branched flower stalks carry nodding orange-pink blooms in fall, well above the foliage. Water thoroughly and then let the soil dry completely before watering again, and keep water out of the crown of the rosette to prevent rot. Like other large hybrid echeverias, it is propagated only by stem cuttings and offsets rather than from seed.

common_name: Morning Beauty Echeveria (Frosted Lavender-Pink Ruffled Hybrid)

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, well-drained succulent mix in full sun to bright light; cooler temperatures and strong light intensify the pastel coloring.

directions: This popular hybrid forms a dense rosette of broad, gently ruffled leaves coated in a soft, powdery bloom that shifts from pale blue-green in warm weather to lavender-pink and rose along the margins as temperatures cool. It offsets readily around the base, building into a tidy cluster useful for mixed succulent containers and dish gardens. Water deeply and allow the soil to dry out completely between waterings, keeping the rosette center dry to avoid rot. Being a named hybrid cultivar, it is propagated vegetatively from offsets or cuttings rather than from seed.

planting.note: Divide and replant offset clusters in spring in shallow, gritty soil in full sun to bright light; this small-growing hybrid is especially well suited to dish gardens and terrariums.

directions: A miniature hybrid cultivar, Mebina produces an abundance of tiny rosettes only an inch or so across, in pale green tipped with coral-pink, that cluster tightly together to form a dense, mounding colony far faster than most echeverias. The small scale and fast offsetting habit make it a favorite for fairy gardens, succulent bowls, and living wreaths. Grow in full sun to bright light in very well-drained soil, watering sparingly and letting the mix dry out completely between waterings. Because the rosettes are so small and shallow-rooted, it dries out faster than larger echeverias and benefits from slightly more frequent light watering in active growth.

common_name: Ruby Chenille Plant (Red-Flushed Fuzzy Echeveria Selection)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; cool nights and strong light bring out the deepest ruby-red color on the fuzzy foliage.

directions: This selection of the chenille plant intensifies the species' signature coating of fine white hairs with a deep ruby-red flush across the leaf surface and margins, most vivid in cool weather and bright sun. Branching, shrubby stems carry rounded, fuzzy leaves and produce red-and-yellow bell-shaped flowers in winter and early spring. Water thoroughly and then allow the soil to dry out completely before watering again, taking care not to wet the hairy foliage excessively, since trapped moisture can cause spotting. It roots easily from stem cuttings and old plants can be cut back hard to encourage fresh, more compact branching.

common_name: Red Edge Echeveria (Green Rosette with Thin Red-Margined Leaves)

planting.note: Plant offsets or root leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, well-drained cactus mix in full sun; strong light keeps the margin color crisp and the leaves compact.

directions: A widely grown selection of the agavoides group, Red Edge forms a tight, symmetrical rosette of thick, triangular, apple-green leaves tipped with a fine, sharp point and outlined in a thin line of red along the margins. The contrast sharpens in bright, cool conditions and fades somewhat in shade or heavy heat. Coral-pink and yellow bell-shaped flowers appear on arching stalks in spring. Grow in sharply drained soil in full sun, water deeply and then let the mix dry out completely, and propagate from offsets or individual leaves.
